title: AI sell-off: strong demand vs. funding needs
summary: Is the recent AI sell-off about weakening demand, or growing doubts over how the investment boom will be funded?
body_markdown:
# AI sell-off: strong demand vs. funding needs


Julien Lafargue, Chief Market Strategist


2 November 2026


**Share this Insight**

**Please note: The article does not constitute advice or any form of recommendation.**


## Key points


-


Volatility is back: the Nasdaq 100 is nearing correction territory


-


AI demand remains strong. What the market is questioning is funding, as hyperscalers keep lifting capex while free cash flow evaporates


-


Investors are stepping away from AI as a whole rather than rotating within it, but positioning is still heavy and the funding loop remains intact


-


Hiding in defensives is tempting but, for multi-asset investors, it largely means doubling down on bond exposure.


Since mid-October, the AI trade has gone from market engine to market problem. Nothing suggests demand for AI is fading, but investors are now questioning who will pay for the build-out, and how. Until that question gets a better answer or positioning has cleared, rebounds may be tentative. Encouragingly, this process is also strengthening the foundations on which a subsequent rally could build.


## A regime change in volatility


US equities entered mid-October after 53 trading sessions without a 1% daily fall in the S&P 500. Three weeks later, the Nasdaq 100 has suffered three declines of 2.5%–3.5%. Its only sizeable rebound, a 2.8% gain, unravelled within four sessions. The index is now 9.5% below its October high. After a strong rally, that drawdown is hardly extraordinary. What matters is where the selling is concentrated, and why good news has failed to stop it.


## The market is doubting the funding, not the demand


AI fundamentals remain very strong in absolute terms. ASML and TSMC both reported robust AI demand and full backlogs. Schneider Electric, one of the clearest ‘picks and shovels’ plays on data centres, beat expectations and raised guidance. In a healthier market, those results would have lifted the whole complex. This time, none of these stocks managed to hold on to their gains.


When good news stops being rewarded, the debate has usually moved on. Here, it has moved from demand to funding. The AI build-out increasingly relies on outside capital, and the signals from capital markets have turned less friendly. Reports that Anthropic’s IPO valuation had been cut from around $2tn to around $1.5tn mattered for two reasons: a smaller raise means less money flowing into infrastructure, and a lower price for one of the sector’s flagship names puts pressure on AI valuations across the board. Credit markets are telling a similar story. Bonds of the most highly levered AI infrastructure names now yield in the mid-teens, and high yield issuers tied to data centres trade at spreads of roughly 600bp to 1,600bp. That is a small corner of the market, but it is precisely the corner that finances the marginal data centre.


## Hyperscalers are not offering a way out yet


The obvious circuit breaker would have come from the largest spenders. A hyperscaler choosing to cap capex for now, or showing that free cash flow is starting to recover, would go a long way to validating the money already committed. Unfortunately, the latest earnings season delivered neither.


Every major hyperscaler has signalled that capex will rise again next year, in some cases sharply. At the same time, free cash flow is turning negative across the group. Microsoft looks like the exception, but largely because third-party capacity is coming online later than planned. That is a question of timing, and analysts expect the delayed spending to land in the coming quarters.


This creates a self-reinforcing loop. With free cash flow turning negative, even the largest spenders now rely on capital markets to fund the build-out, alongside the AI labs and neoclouds that always have. If funding becomes harder to secure, fewer data centres get built. Fewer data centres mean less capacity to sell, and therefore slower earnings growth, both for hyperscalers and for the companies supplying them. And slower earnings growth makes investors less willing to fund the next round of capex. Until something breaks that loop, the market has little reason to pay up for the growth it is being promised.


## Investors are stepping away from AI as a whole


The way stocks are falling supports this reading. A sell-off in AI can simply be a rotation within the theme, with money moving between chipmakers and platforms. That is not what is happening now: the two are falling together. In mid-October, semiconductors and the ‘Magnificent 7’ fell in tandem for three straight sessions, only the fourth time this year. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) had by then fallen for eight sessions in a row, its longest losing streak since 2008, and it later dropped more than 6% in a single day.


Beyond AI, the market has held up reasonably well. On one of the worst days in mid-October, with the S&P 500 down 1.1%, 248 of its members still finished higher. Over the last month, the equal-weighted S&P 500 rose 5.0% while the market-cap-weighted index fell 0.9%. This is less an endorsement of the rest of the market than a reflection of positioning. Investors can’t sell what they don’t own, so they have moved towards whatever sits furthest from AI.


## Bonds worked. The hiding places may not


The most reassuring development has been in fixed income. Treasuries have done their job as a diversifier: on the sharpest down days, yields fell across the curve, with the US 10-year dropping back below 5%. Notably, this happened even as Brent crude prices rose significantly. Since funding costs are at the centre of the worry, lower yields are a genuine support, although credit spreads matter just as much.


Equity rotation has been less convincing. At first, money flowed into small caps which we felt made little sense: if AI is no longer driving US growth, the cyclicality of US small caps is hardly where one should hide. More recently, the rotation has become more defensive. Small caps fell 1.6% on Friday 30 October, while consumer staples, utilities and healthcare attracted buyers.


That move is understandable, but for multi-asset investors it is less protective than it looks. Defensive sectors, with the possible exception of healthcare, trade much like bonds. Adding them to a portfolio that already holds fixed income effectively doubles down on duration. And if sentiment towards AI improves, that extra defensive tilt could become a drag at exactly the wrong moment.


## Where this leaves us


The best days in equity markets often follow the worst ones, and further sharp rebounds are likely. But we doubt they will last until the funding question is addressed. At the same time, positioning hasn’t yet fully cleared out, in our opinion. The good news is that there is a self-balancing mechanism at play. Indeed, the data centre boom depends on raising capital, so as valuations fall, spending will be forced down to what can actually be funded. Growth may be slower in the short term, but it would rest on firmer ground, with free cash flow recovering and less reliance on capital markets. We are not there yet. But once investors can see that path, we expect the AI theme to find a second wind.
